transcript.text: Our Henry has gone a bit weak and sounds rough, sort of rattly growl instead of the normal hum. It's about 12 years old. Bags and filter are new. Worth fixing?

At 12 years old, with new bags and filters already in place, that 'rough rattly growl' combined with weak suction points strongly towards the motor itself. Specifically, it sounds like the motor bearings are wearing out or there is debris caught inside the fan housing. This is a common failure point for older vacuums as the internal components degrade. Before we consider if repair is viable, I need to rule out a simple blockage that might be causing the strain and noise. Please detach the hose from the main body of the vacuum (with it switched off and unplugged) and look through it, plus check the wand and floorhead neck. If you can drop a coin through and have it fall straight out, the airway is clear. Regarding whether it's worth fixing: if this is indeed worn motor bearings, the repair usually involves checking the entire motor unit. For a 12-year-old vacuum, that cost often approaches or exceeds the value of the machine, making replacement the more sensible option unless you have a specific fondness for this model or it's a high-end commercial unit. Let me know if the airway is clear.
[Helpful to see: image "Poor suction — what to check first" — Lost suction is usually a full bin, a dirty filter or a blockage in the hose, tube or floor head — check and clear those before suspecting the motor. Switch off and unplug first. Typical layout — your model may differ.]
I've checked the hose by dropping a coin through it and it goes straight through, so the airway seems clear. What should I check next?

Since the airway is clear and the bags/filters are new, the 'rattly growl' combined with weak suction points to the motor itself. At 12 years old, the most likely culprit is worn motor bearings. As they wear, the motor shaft wobbles, creating that rough noise and reducing efficiency (weak suction). A secondary possibility is debris caught in the fan housing, which can also cause rattling and block airflow. To confirm this:
1. Unplug the vacuum.
2. 3. Spin the fan blade by hand. It should spin freely and quietly. If it grinds, feels gritty, or wobbles, the bearings are shot.
4. Check for any debris stuck to the fan blades. If the fan is rough or noisy when spun by hand, the motor needs replacing. Given the age of the vacuum, this is often not cost-effective compared to buying a new one, unless you have a specific reason to keep it.

I'm afraid I'm not confident taking the motor out, and I only have a screwdriver, so I'm not sure how I'd get at the fan to spin it. I should have mentioned that after about five minutes it gives off a hot, burning electrical smell. When I looked at the exhaust grille on top in the dim hall, I also saw what looked like blue-orange sparks flickering inside. Is that important?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. Yes, that is very important. Blue-orange sparks and a burning electrical smell inside the machine are serious safety hazards. It indicates an internal electrical fault—likely worn carbon brushes or damaged motor windings causing arcing. Because of this active hazard, you must stop using the vacuum immediately. Do not plug it in again until a qualified engineer has inspected it. Given the age (12 years) and these specific symptoms, repair is rarely cost-effective compared to replacement, but for safety reasons, please do not attempt any internal checks yourself. If you are considering buying a new one, I can help you compare options once this one is safely stored away.
[Panel: "To check a suitable replacement — Enter your model number below. Once we have the model I can check whether a suitable replacement is available. It's usually on a sticker inside the door or around the frame, or on the back of the appliance."]
